findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized query parameter passed to Process.Start
findings.description: Ping() binds an attacker-controlled value from [FromQuery] string host and concatenates it directly into the argument string handed to Process.Start("cmd.exe", "/c ping -n 1 " + host). The value flows from an HTTP query parameter into a shell (cmd.exe /c) with no validation, quoting or escaping, so a payload such as '127.0.0.1 & whoami' or '127.0.0.1 & powershell -enc ...' is executed with the web process identity. No argument list API or allow-list is used, so this is a genuine tainted flow into a command-execution sink.

## Analysis: model-46f74f672f3ca92d

**Confirmed at source level.** `app/VulnCmd.cs` is 7 lines and contains exactly the pattern described:

```csharp
public class VulnCmdController : Controller {
    public void Ping([FromQuery] string host) {
        Process.Start("cmd.exe", "/c ping -n 1 " + host);
    }
}
```

The tainted flow is complete and short: `[FromQuery] string host` (model binding from the query string) → string concatenation → `Process.Start("cmd.exe", ...)`. Because the argument list begins with `/c`, `cmd.exe` parses the remainder as a shell command line, so metacharacters in `host` (`&`, `|`, `^`, `>`, `` ` ``) are interpreted by the shell rather than passed as literal ping arguments. `127.0.0.1 & whoami` executes `whoami` under the IIS/ASP.NET worker identity. This matches the first CWE-78 subtype described by MITRE: a fixed program with attacker-controlled argument content, where separator characters are not neutralized.

findings.title: Insecure BinaryFormatter deserialization of untrusted stream (RCE gadget chain)
findings.description: Load(Stream body) passes a caller-supplied stream straight into BinaryFormatter.Deserialize with no type restriction, binder, or serialization guard. BinaryFormatter is documented by Microsoft as unsafe and removed in .NET 8+ precisely because deserializing attacker-controlled bytes enables gadget-chain remote code execution and arbitrary object instantiation. The stream has no validation, size limit or trusted-source check, and the method is public on a plain class, making it a reachable deserialization entry point.

findings.title: SQL injection via string concatenation into SqlCommand query
findings.description: Find() takes [FromQuery] string user and builds the query text by concatenation: "SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Name = '" + user + "'". No SqlParameter is added, so a value such as ' OR '1'='1' -- or a UNION payload can alter the executed statement, allowing authentication bypass and full-table data exfiltration. Contrast with SafeSql.cs, which uses the same shape but binds @u through AddWithValue and is therefore not vulnerable.

findings.title: Stored/reflected XSS via @Html.Raw on unencoded model data
findings.description: The view renders Model.Bio with @Html.Raw, which writes the value to the response without HTML encoding. Bio is a user-profile field, so any attacker-supplied content (profile bio, comment, imported data) executes as script in every viewer's browser, enabling session theft and account takeover. SafeView.cshtml renders the same field with the default @Model.Bio encoding and is correctly protected.

## Assessment: confirmed vulnerable code, unconfirmed reachability

**What the source shows.** `app/VulnDeser.cs` is 8 lines. `Load(Stream body)` constructs a `BinaryFormatter` and returns `fmt.Deserialize(body)` (line 6). The stream parameter is passed directly into the deserializer with no `SerializationBinder`, no type allow-list, no size limit, and no validation of any kind. Microsoft's own documentation states the method "is never safe when used with untrusted input" and describes a successful attack as the equivalent of "interpreting that payload as a standalone executable and launching it." The .NET 9 runtime now throws on any in-box `BinaryFormatter` use.

The "safe" counterpart named in the finding, `SafeJson.cs`, is a separate class using `System.Text.Json` and does not mitigate anything here -- the two files are unrelated in the call graph. That part of the scanner's narrative is misleading, but the sink itself is real.

**Where the evidence stops.** There is no caller of `VulnDeser.Load` anywhere in the snapshot. A repo-wide grep for `VulnDeser` and `.Load(` returns only the class declaration itself.
